course_details.Overview of class: The modern Big Bang perspective on the origin, structure, evolution, and fate of the universe. Topics to be discussed include the extragalactic distance scale, the Hubble expansion, the large-scale clustering of galaxies, cosmic inflation and the early universe, Big Bang nucleosynthesis, the cosmic microwave background radiation, dark matter, dark energy, and the recent evidence for acceleration in the expansion of the universe. This WCAS FD-NS course (formerly called Area 1) is designed for non-science majors, but all are welcome

course_details.Overview of class:
We will discuss a book in class, with one discussion leader assigned to each meeting, which will be held twice a week. The book is written for non-experts interested in the topic of cosmology.

The book approaches cosmology from a historical perspective and demonstrates how, time after time, previously accepted worldviews were proven incorrect. Today, on the one hand, cosmologists have developed a model that fits together beautifully. On the other hand, its agreement with observations depends on invoking Dark Energy and Dark Matter, neither of which has been verified in a laboratory. The book asks the question: "Based on history, are we sure we have the correct model now?"

The alternative theory proposed by the author is too complex for this course and is therefore replaced with a set of recent articles written for non-experts. These additional articles challenge the book's theme that astronomers today have completely accepted the so-called concordance model of cosmology, which includes Dark Energy and Dark Matter.

In addition to being a useful resource for learning basic astronomy and cosmology, the book demonstrates, by example, how to analyze cosmological models and is therefore an excellent resource for developing critical-thinking skills.

The book is: Facts and Speculations in Cosmology by Jayant Narlikar.
course_details.Evaluation Method:
Students will write three original papers based on the book readings. Paper 3 should be written specifically to address the WCAS Writing Place Rubrics. An additional graded assignment will be a revision of either Paper 1 or Paper 2.

Students will also be required to give a 10-minute presentation at the end of the quarter based on the paper of their choice. This presentation will be graded.

course_details.Overview of class: This course is an introduction to planets and planetary systems. We will learn about the structure, origin, and evolution of planets---including both the planets in the Solar System and the many recently discovered extrasolar planets.
course_details.Registration Requirements: The course is intended for advanced undergraduates and graduate students. Students are expected to have taken year-long courses in calculus and physics. Classical Mechanics at the level of Physics 330-1,2 is strongly encouraged. Students should also know a bit of computer programming, or be prepared to learn.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
-The dynamical processes through which planets form and evolve
-The physics of planetary atmospheres and interiors
-The techniques to detect and characterize other worlds, including the search for life
course_details.Evaluation Method: Evaluation will be based on assignments, class participation, and exams

course_details.Overview of class: This course explores the underlying physical processes at play during the lives and deaths of stars. Basic principles and mathematical theory that govern the interiors, atmospheres and evolution of stars will be presented. Topics to be covered include pre-main sequence evolution, main sequence evolution, red giant and asymptotic branch phases, and white dwarfs and neutron stars.

course_details.Overview of class: The class aims to provide insight into how processes involving interstellar and intergalactic gas and dust are treated, including interpreting absorption and emission lines, absorption and emission by dust, continuum radio emission, interstellar magnetic fields, supernova remnants, and formation of stars and planets in molecular clouds. A key component of the class is the independent research project, for which students work in small groups to apply concepts and techniques learned to topics that relate to their anticipated Ph.D. research areas.
course_details.Teaching Method: Several class meetings per week, problem sets, and independent research project.
course_details.Evaluation Method: Class participation, problem sets, and the independent research project which includes both a written report and a class presentation near the end of the quarter.
